questions.title: How can the D.C. Circuit throw out the case for lack of standing after the district court already ruled on the merits?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. The district court interpreted the statutes, said OSC made a legal error, remanded to the agency, and only later entered final judgment. On appeal, the D.C. Circuit says AFL lacked Article III standing all along and vacates the district court's judgment with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Can an appellate court raise standing on its own even if neither party briefed it at first? And if standing was missing from the start, does that mean the district court had no power to issue any merits ruling at all?

questions.title: Why doesn't a statute saying OSC 'shall conduct an investigation' automatically give the requester standing to sue?
questions.question_body: Section 1216(a)(3) uses mandatory language: OSC 'shall' investigate allegations of arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholding. My instinct was that if Congress creates that duty, then the person who filed the allegation should be able to sue when OSC refuses. But the court says a 'procedural right in vacuo' is not enough under Article III. What exactly is missing here? Is the problem that Congress can create a statutory duty, but cannot eliminate the need for a separate concrete injury?

questions.title: Why did the court say AFL's FOIA-records injury was caused by DOJ rather than by OSC's refusal to investigate?
questions.question_body: AFL argued that OSC's failure to investigate prevented it from getting the records it requested from DOJ. The court rejects that on causation grounds and says any informational injury from nondisclosure is 'plainly traceable to DOJ—not OSC.' I'm having trouble with that because AFL's whole theory is that OSC enforcement might pressure DOJ employees to comply. Is the rule basically that the immediate withholder of records is the legally relevant cause, and a regulator's failure to police that conduct is too indirect?

questions.title: Why wasn't redressability satisfied if the requested remedy was only an order requiring OSC to investigate?
questions.question_body: The opinion says AFL's theory depended on a speculative chain: OSC might investigate, might pursue corrective or disciplinary action, MSPB might impose sanctions, and then DOJ might produce records. I understand that chain is long, but in procedural-right cases I thought courts relax redressability somewhat. So why wasn't that enough here? Is it mainly because the result depended on discretionary choices by OSC, MSPB, and DOJ, all of which are independent actors not before the court?

questions.title: How are 5 U.S.C. § 1216 and FOIA's disciplinary provision in § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) supposed to interact?
questions.question_body: OSC refused to investigate because FOIA's own enforcement provision, § 552(a)(4)(F)(i), is triggered only when a court orders production, awards fees, and specifically questions whether the withholding was arbitrary or capricious. But AFL argued that § 1216 independently requires OSC to investigate alleged FOIA violations even without those predicates, and the district court agreed. What is the best way to read these two provisions together? Is § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) a narrow mandatory trigger that supplements a broader § 1216 authority, or is it supposed to be the exclusive route for OSC involvement in FOIA withholding cases?

questions.title: Why didn't AFL have informational standing based on the notices and updates it said OSC should have provided?
questions.question_body: The court says informational standing exists only when a plaintiff is denied information that a statute actually entitles him to receive. AFL argued that if OSC had investigated under § 1216, it could have received the kinds of notices and information described in § 1214. But the court says that isn't enough because OSC was not required to graft § 1214's notice provisions onto a § 1216 investigation. Is the key distinction here between a guaranteed disclosure right and a mere possibility of receiving information if the agency chooses to follow a certain procedure?

questions.title: Does § 1216(c)'s phrase 'in the same way as if a prohibited personnel practice were involved' import § 1214 procedures or only the available remedies?
questions.question_body: I'm stuck on the statutory language in § 1216(c). It says OSC may investigate and seek corrective action under § 1214 and disciplinary action under § 1215 'in the same way as if a prohibited personnel practice were involved.' AFL seemed to rely on that language to argue for investigation-related rights, while the court cites cases saying OSC's choice whether to follow § 1214 procedures in a § 1216 investigation is discretionary. Does 'in the same way' mean the whole § 1214 procedural framework comes along, or does it just mean OSC can use the same enforcement mechanisms without being bound to all the same procedural steps?
